options.text: The heating effect of an electric current
The creation of a magnetic field by a permanent magnet
The force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field
The generation of a voltage by changing the magnetic flux through a conductor

questions.explanation: Electromagnetic induction is the process of generating a voltage (and current in a complete circuit) when a conductor experiences a changing magnetic field or moves through a magnetic field.

questions.stem: A magnet is held stationary inside a coil of wire connected to a galvanometer. What voltage is induced?

options.text: Zero voltage
A large voltage
A small constant voltage
An alternating voltage

questions.explanation: No voltage is induced when the magnet is stationary because there is no change in magnetic flux through the coil. A voltage is only induced when the flux is changing, which requires relative movement or a changing field.

questions.stem: Which of the following will NOT increase the induced voltage when moving a magnet into a coil?

options.text: Using a stronger magnet
Using a thicker wire for the coil
Moving the magnet faster
Increasing the number of turns on the coil

questions.explanation: Using thicker wire does not increase the induced voltage. The induced voltage increases with faster movement, a stronger magnet, more turns on the coil, or adding an iron core.

options.text: The induced current is always proportional to the resistance
The induced current always flows in a direction that opposes the change that caused it
The induced current always flows in the same direction as the magnetic field
The induced current always helps the motion that caused it

questions.explanation: Lenz's law states that the direction of the induced current is always such that it opposes the change producing it. This is a consequence of conservation of energy.

questions.stem: Fleming's right-hand rule is used for which situation?

options.text: Finding the direction of induced current (generators)
Finding the force on a current-carrying wire (motors)
Finding the poles of a solenoid
Finding the direction of electron flow

questions.explanation: Fleming's right-hand rule is used for the generator effect (electromagnetic induction) to find the direction of the induced current. Fleming's left-hand rule is used for the motor effect.

questions.stem: A north pole is pushed towards a coil. According to Lenz's law, what pole does the near end of the coil become?

options.text: South pole
It has no polarity
North pole
It alternates between north and south

questions.explanation: By Lenz's law, the induced current must oppose the approaching north pole. The near end of the coil becomes a north pole to repel the approaching magnet, opposing the motion.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an application of electromagnetic induction?

options.text: A filament light bulb
An electric generator at a power station
An electric heater
A battery

questions.explanation: Generators use electromagnetic induction to produce electricity. A coil is rotated in a magnetic field, causing a continuous change in magnetic flux that induces a voltage, which is how most of the world's electricity is produced.
